entry.reasons: The entry accurately reflects the essential knowledge statements 2.5.A.2 and 2.5.A.3 from the AP Physics 1 CED, specifically regarding the direction of the acceleration of a system's center of mass and the condition under which its velocity changes.

Topic 2.5.A.2 states that the acceleration of a system’s center of mass is “in the same direction as that net force.” Topic 2.5.A.3 states that its velocity “will only change if a nonzero net external force is exerted on that system.” The entry accurately states both requirements using CED wording; no caution is needed.

a_factual: The body matches the CED. 2.5.A.2 states the acceleration of a system's center of mass 'is in the same direction as that net force', and 2.5.A.3 states 'The velocity of a system's center of mass will only change if a nonzero net external force is exerted on that system.' The body's first clause drops the magnitude-proportionality part of 2.5.A.2, but what it asserts is accurate and the omission does not make it false. b_topic_codes: 2.5 (Newton's Second Law) is where these statements are first required, and the owner and only topic code are both 2.5. c_ced_required: 2.5.A.2 and 2.5.A.3 are essential knowledge statements under LO 2.5.A that a student must reproduce and apply. d_caution: The body's wording is a faithful restatement of the CED phrasing ('same direction as that net force'; 'only change if a nonzero net external force'), so the wording that earns the point is present and no caution is needed. caution is null, which is correct.

The entry accurately reflects the requirements of Topic 2.2 (Forces and Free-Body Diagrams), specifically EK 2.2.B.1 through 2.2.B.4 and the accompanying boundary statement regarding drawing individual forces as straight arrows originating on the dot, side-by-side if in the same direction, and avoiding components.

Topic 2.2 is the first required treatment of free-body diagrams. EK 2.2.B.2 says a free-body diagram shows each force exerted on an object or system by the environment; 2.2.B.3 places force vectors at the center-of-mass representation. EK 2.2.B.4 supports the coordinate-axis guidance. The boundary statement requires individual straight arrows originating on the dot, same-direction forces side by side rather than overlapping, and forces rather than force components. The caution accurately preserves those requirements.

a_factual: The body matches 2.2.B.2 ('The free-body diagram of an object or system shows each of the forces exerted on the object by the environment') and 2.2.B.3 (forces are vectors originating from the center-of-mass representation, 'such as a dot'). The items match the Topic 2.2 boundary statement: individual straight arrows originating on the dot, same-direction forces drawn side by side and not overlapping, whole forces rather than components, and 2.2.B.4 (one axis parallel to the direction of acceleration, e.g., parallel to an incline). b_topic_codes: Topic 2.2 is where the FBD is first introduced (the unit overview calls it 'the introduction of the free-body diagram'), and 2.2 is the only listed code, which uses it. c_ced_required: LO 2.2.B ('Describe the forces exerted on an object or system using a free-body diagram') and 2.2.B.1 ('Free-body diagrams are useful tools for visualizing forces...') require students to apply this. d_caution: The body omits the side-by-side and no-component rules that the CED boundary statement makes point-earning; the caution supplies both and correctly cites the Topic 2.2 boundary statement. Minor note, not a failing point: the ced_evidence quote is a truncated paraphrase of the boundary statement, and its wording is not verbatim.

The entry accurately represents Newton's second law for a system as described in Topic 2.5 (specifically EK 2.5.A.2 and 2.5.A.3). The topic codes are correct as Newton's second law is introduced in 2.5 and applied to gravitational force in 2.6 and circular motion in 2.9.

Topic 2.5.A.2 states that the acceleration of a system’s center of mass is proportional to the net force and points in its direction; 2.5.A.3 specifies a “nonzero net external force.” Topic 2.5 first requires the relationship. Topics 2.6 and 2.9 also apply it to gravitational and circular motion. The caution correctly identifies the system and the external-force sum.

a_factual: The body a_cm = ΣF_ext/m_sys is the standard form of the relation in CED 2.5.A.2, 'the acceleration of a system's center of mass has a magnitude proportional to the magnitude of the net force exerted on the system and is in the same direction as that net force.' The symbols match: a_cm is the center-of-mass acceleration, the sum is over external forces, and m_sys is the system mass. The CED 'Relevant equation' is rendered as an image that does not survive text extraction, so this check rests on the standard form and the caution's citation of 2.5.A.3. b_topic_codes: 2.5 is the first unit-2 topic that states Newton's second law (2.5.A.2), so it is the correct owner. 2.6 uses it for apparent weight when the system accelerates (2.6.C.2: 'If the system is accelerating, the apparent weight of the system is not equal to the magnitude of the gravitational force'). 2.9 uses it for centripetal acceleration (2.9.A.1.i, a_c = v²/r, requires net force). The 2.6 link is the weaker of the two, but it is a real use within this unit. c_ced_required: 2.5.A.2 and 2.5.A.3 ('The velocity of a system's center of mass will only change if a nonzero net external force is exerted on that system') require students to apply this relation. d_caution: The CED wording is proportionality of magnitudes plus same direction, not an equality with a sum of external forces. The caution states the CED wording correctly and ties the sum to 2.5.A.3. The caution is present and correct. hooks: none supplied, so no hook checks apply.
The entry accurately represents the derived equation for weight as specified in Topic 2.6 (Essential Knowledge 2.6.A.3) of the AP Physics 1 CED: 'Weight = Fg = mg'.

Topic 2.6.A.3 defines weight as the gravitational force exerted by an astronomical body on a relatively small nearby object and gives the derived equation “Weight = Fg = mg.” The entry reproduces that equation, is correctly assigned to Topic 2.6, and needs no caution.

a_factual: CED 2.6.A.3 defines weight as 'the gravitational force exerted by an astronomical body on a relatively small nearby object' and lists the derived equation 'Weight = Fg = mg'. The body \text{Weight}=F_g=mg matches the symbols and order exactly. b_topic_codes: 2.6.A.3 appears under Topic 2.6 (Gravitational Force), so owner_topic_code '2.6' is correct, and topic_codes ['2.6'] is the only topic that uses it. c_ced_required: 2.6.A.3 is an essential-knowledge statement that includes this derived equation, so a student is required to apply it. d_caution: the CED wording 'Weight = Fg = mg' is the same as the entry, so the point-earning wording is matched and no caution is needed (caution null is correct). The entry's ced_evidence quotation is accurate. Hooks: none present, so no hook checks apply.
The definition of normal force is highly factual and matches 2.7.A.2.ii. The topic codes are correct and belong to Unit 2. The caution is accurate and references 2.9.A.2.i correctly.

The body matches 2.7.A.2.ii: normal force is the perpendicular component of the surface's force and is directed away from the surface. The caution is consistent with 2.9.A.2.i, which says that at the minimum speed at the top of a vertical loop, gravitational force is the only force causing centripetal acceleration. All three listed topics use normal force, but 2.6.C.1 first requires it: 'The magnitude of the apparent weight of a system is the magnitude of the normal force exerted on the system.' The owner_topic_code should therefore be 2.6, not 2.7.
